hero.eyebrow: Document skills · No software to install
hero.title: Microsoft Word: learn by doing
hero.subtitle: Write letters, résumés and reports in a working document editor inside your browser. Every task is checked and explained.
hero.outcomeLine: After this course you can produce a clear, professional document for school, work or study.

outcomes.title: Edit with confidence
outcomes.text: Select, copy, undo and find and replace like an experienced user.

outcomes.title: Format well
outcomes.text: Fonts, spacing, alignment and lists that make text easy to read.

outcomes.title: Structure documents
outcomes.text: Heading styles, page setup, headers, footers and page numbers.

outcomes.title: Use tables and pictures
outcomes.text: Line up data in tables and place pictures with captions and alt text.

outcomes.title: Write professional documents
outcomes.text: Letters, résumés, reports and meeting minutes.

outcomes.title: Review and share
outcomes.text: Proofread, track changes, make documents accessible and export a PDF.

assessment: Finish the required labs in each module: they are checked automatically and explained when something is missing.
Pass each module quiz (70% or more). You can retry as often as you like.
Complete the final report and the final assessment.

faq.q: Do I need Microsoft Word installed?
faq.a: No. The labs run in your browser. The skills carry over to Word, Google Docs and LibreOffice Writer.
About six and a half hours, in short sessions.
Finishing every module and the final assessment marks the course complete on your GrowQR profile.

activities.title: Write and save your first document
activities.objective: Type, edit and organise a short document with a title and three paragraphs.
activities.scenario: Your class is making a welcome booklet for new students. Write a short page called 'Welcome to our class'.
steps: Type a title on the first line.
Write three short paragraphs: who we are, what we do each week, and what we hope for this year.
Read it through and fix any typing mistakes.

checks.label: A title at the top that includes the word Welcome
checks.hint: Type the title on the first line, such as Welcome to our class.
checks.explain: A title tells the reader what the page is about before they read a word.

checks.label: Three paragraphs of at least 12 words each
checks.hint: Press Enter between paragraphs and write a full sentence or two in each.
checks.explain: One idea per paragraph keeps a page easy to read.

checks.label: At least 70 words in total
checks.hint: Add a little more detail to each paragraph.
checks.explain: A short page still needs enough words to say something useful.

activities.title: Format an event flyer
activities.objective: Use bold, centring, a larger title and a list to make a flyer easy to scan.
activities.scenario: The school library is holding a book fair. Format the plain text below into a flyer people can read from a distance.
steps: Make the title larger and centre it.
Make the date and place bold.
Turn the three activities into a bulleted list.
Centre the last line.

checks.label: The title is a different size
checks.hint: Select the title and choose a larger font size.
checks.explain: Size shows which text matters most.

checks.label: Something is centred
checks.hint: Select the title and use the centre button.
checks.explain: Centred text suits short titles and notices.

checks.label: The date and place are bold
checks.hint: Select the line and press B.
checks.explain: Bold draws the eye to the facts people need.

checks.label: A bulleted list with three items
checks.hint: Select the three activities and press the bullet-list button.
checks.explain: A list is quicker to scan than a paragraph.

checks.label: The words are still there
checks.hint: Formatting should not delete any of the text.
checks.explain: Formatting changes how text looks, not what it says.

initial.html:

activities.title: Rescue a messy draft
activities.objective: Tidy a draft by fixing mistakes and applying consistent formatting.
activities.scenario: A friend sent you a rough note. It has spelling mistakes and no structure. Make it clear and professional.
steps: Fix the three spelling mistakes (recieve, tommorow, seperate).
Make the first line a heading.
Turn the things to bring into a numbered list.

checks.label: recieve is corrected
checks.hint: The correct spelling is receive (i before e, except after c).
checks.explain: A remembered rule helps: i before e, except after c.

checks.label: tommorow is corrected
checks.hint: Tomorrow has one m and two r.
checks.explain: Careful typing and a spell check catch most slips.

checks.label: seperate is corrected
checks.hint: Separate has the letters pa in the middle.
checks.explain: Words with a tricky middle are easy to mistype.

checks.label: The first line is a heading
checks.hint: Choose Heading 1 for the first line.
checks.explain: A heading makes the structure clear at a glance.

checks.label: A numbered list of three items
checks.hint: Select the three things to bring and press the numbered-list button.
checks.explain: A numbered list suits things to check off.

initial.html:
Trip details

We will recieve the bus tickets tommorow and the groups will travel in seperate buses.

Your school ID

A packed lunch

A bottle of water

activities.title: Outline a report with headings
activities.objective: Build a clear structure with a title, headings and subheadings.
activities.scenario: You are writing a short report on water use at school. Plan its structure before writing the detail.
steps: Write the title as a Heading 1.
Add three main sections as Heading 2: Introduction, Findings, Recommendations.
Add two subheadings (Heading 3) under Findings.
Write at least one sentence under each section.

checks.label: One main title (Heading 1)
checks.hint: Choose Heading 1 for the title line.
checks.explain: There should be one main title per document.

checks.label: At least three Heading 2 sections
checks.hint: Use Heading 2 for the three main sections.
checks.explain: Heading 2 marks the main parts of the report.

checks.label: At least two Heading 3 subheadings
checks.hint: Use Heading 3 under Findings.
checks.explain: Subheadings break a long section into smaller pieces.

checks.label: Sections appear in order
checks.hint: Introduction, then Findings, then Recommendations.
checks.explain: A logical order helps the reader follow your argument.

checks.label: Real sentences under the headings
checks.hint: Write at least three paragraphs with ten words or more.
checks.explain: Headings organise the report; the sentences carry the content.

activities.title: Make a weekly timetable table
activities.objective: Insert a table and fill it so the information lines up in rows and columns.
activities.scenario: A study group needs a timetable for the week, with a row for each day and columns for morning and afternoon.
steps: Add a heading called Study timetable.
Insert a table with at least 4 rows and 3 columns.
Fill the header row with Day, Morning and Afternoon.
Write a subject in every other cell.

checks.label: A heading called Study timetable
checks.hint: Type the title and make it a heading.
checks.explain: A table without a title leaves the reader guessing.

checks.label: A table of at least 4 rows by 3 columns
checks.hint: Use the Table button and choose 4 rows and 3 columns.
checks.explain: Tables line up information that has more than one dimension.

checks.label: The header row names the columns
checks.hint: Type Day, Morning and Afternoon in the first row.
checks.explain: Column headings explain what each column holds.

spec.what: the column headings Day, Morning and Afternoon

checks.label: Some text is bold
checks.hint: Select the header row and press B.
checks.explain: Bold headers set the labels apart from the data.

activities.title: Write a formal letter
activities.objective: Lay out a formal letter with a date, greeting, clear paragraphs, a list and a polite closing.
activities.scenario: You are asking the school librarian for permission to run a reading club after school on Fridays.
steps: Start with a date.
Greet the reader: Dear Ms Rao.
Write three short paragraphs: your request, why it helps, and what you need.
Add a bulleted list of three things you need.
Close with Yours sincerely and your name in bold.

checks.label: A date near the top
checks.hint: Write a date such as 12 March 2026.
checks.explain: A date shows when the letter was written.

checks.label: A greeting starting Dear
checks.hint: Begin the letter body with Dear and the person's name.
checks.explain: A greeting is polite and tells the reader who the letter is for.

checks.label: Three paragraphs of real sentences
checks.hint: Each should have at least ten words.
checks.explain: Short paragraphs, each with one purpose, are easy to follow.

checks.label: A bulleted list of at least three needs
checks.hint: Use the bullet button for your three requests.
checks.explain: A list makes requests easy to tick off.

checks.label: A closing: Yours sincerely
checks.hint: Finish with Yours sincerely and your name.
checks.explain: A closing phrase ends the letter politely.

checks.label: Your name or the closing is bold
checks.hint: Select your name and press B.
checks.explain: Bold makes the signature stand out.

activities.title: Build a one-page résumé
activities.objective: Create a clean résumé with a name heading, section headings and bullet lists.
activities.scenario: A student is applying for a summer internship in a library. Build their résumé.
steps: Put the name at the top as a centred heading.
Add section headings: Summary, Skills, Education.
Write a two-sentence summary.
List at least four skills as bullets.
Add an education line.

checks.label: The name is a heading and centred
checks.hint: Make the name a heading, then centre it.
checks.explain: The name is the first thing a recruiter looks for.

checks.label: Three section headings
checks.hint: Use Heading 2 for Summary, Skills and Education.
checks.explain: Clear sections let a recruiter scan in seconds.

checks.label: At least four skills in a list
checks.hint: Use the bullet button.
checks.explain: Skills in a list are easier to scan than in a paragraph.

checks.label: An Education section
checks.hint: Add the heading Education and one line under it.
checks.explain: Education matters most for a student with little work history.

checks.label: Between 80 and 250 words
checks.hint: A one-page résumé is short.
checks.explain: Recruiters spend seconds on each résumé, so brevity matters.

activities.title: Record meeting minutes
activities.objective: Write minutes with a clear header, a numbered list of decisions and a table of actions.
activities.scenario: The student council met today. Record who attended, what was decided and who does what next.
steps: Write the heading Minutes of the student council meeting and the date.
List three decisions in a numbered list.
Add an action table with at least 3 rows and 2 columns: Action and Owner.

checks.label: A heading with Minutes in it
checks.hint: Use a heading for the title.
checks.explain: Minutes are a formal record, so they start with a clear title.

checks.label: A date
checks.hint: Write the date of the meeting.
checks.explain: Minutes without a date are hard to file.

checks.label: Three decisions in a numbered list
checks.hint: Use the numbered-list button.
checks.explain: Numbering makes decisions easy to refer to later.

checks.label: An action table (3 rows by 2 columns)
checks.hint: Insert a table with columns Action and Owner.
checks.explain: A table shows who is responsible for what.

activities.title: Which file format?
activities.objective: Choose a sensible file format for each situation.
activities.scenario: The same document can be saved in different formats. Pick the one that fits.
steps: Read each situation.
Choose the format.
Press Check my work.

checks.label: Item 1 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: A Word document keeps the formatting and lets others edit.

checks.label: Item 2 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: A PDF keeps layout fixed, whatever device opens it.

checks.label: Item 3 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Plain text has no formatting and opens anywhere.

checks.label: Item 4 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: PDFs are the usual choice for finished, read-only documents.

checks.label: Item 5 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: While you are working, use the editable format.

checks.label: Item 6 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Plain text is tiny because it holds only characters.

items.text: You want a friend to edit your essay and suggest changes
items.why: A Word document keeps the formatting and lets others edit.

items.text: You are emailing a final CV that should look the same on every screen
items.why: A PDF keeps layout fixed, whatever device opens it.

items.text: You want to copy notes into a tiny program that only reads text
items.why: Plain text has no formatting and opens anywhere.

items.text: You are submitting a certificate scan to a website
items.why: PDFs are the usual choice for finished, read-only documents.

items.text: You are still drafting a report and will edit it tomorrow
items.why: While you are working, use the editable format.

items.text: You want a file that is as small and simple as possible
items.why: Plain text is tiny because it holds only characters.

activities.title: Style or manual formatting?
activities.objective: Tell good document habits from bad ones.
activities.scenario: Some habits make a document easy to change and easy to navigate. Others cause trouble later.
steps: Read each habit.
Choose Good habit or Causes trouble.
Press Check my work.

checks.label: Item 1 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Styles let you navigate, restyle and build a contents list automatically.

checks.label: Item 2 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Manual formatting is slow and inconsistent; use a Heading style.

checks.label: Item 3 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Empty lines move around when text changes. Use a page break.

checks.label: Item 4 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Real lists keep their spacing and numbering when edited.

checks.label: Item 5 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Fake lists do not indent or renumber properly.

checks.label: Item 6 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: A table keeps columns aligned, whatever the text length.

checks.label: Item 7 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Spaces fall out of line as soon as the text changes.

checks.label: Item 8 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Consistency looks professional and reads easily.

items.text: Use the Heading styles for every section title
items.why: Styles let you navigate, restyle and build a contents list automatically.

items.text: Make a title bigger by typing it, selecting it and picking a font size each time
items.why: Manual formatting is slow and inconsistent; use a Heading style.

items.text: Press Enter many times to push text onto the next page
items.why: Empty lines move around when text changes. Use a page break.

items.text: Use the list button to make a bulleted list
items.why: Real lists keep their spacing and numbering when edited.

items.text: Type a dash or star at the start of each line to fake a list
items.why: Fake lists do not indent or renumber properly.

items.text: Use a table to line up a timetable
items.why: A table keeps columns aligned, whatever the text length.

items.text: Press the space bar many times to line up columns
items.why: Spaces fall out of line as soon as the text changes.

items.text: Use the same font and spacing throughout
items.why: Consistency looks professional and reads easily.

activities.title: Make it accessible
activities.objective: Spot what makes a document easy or hard to read for everyone.
activities.scenario: Accessible documents work for people with low vision, dyslexia or screen readers, and are easier for everyone.
steps: Read each feature.
Choose whether it helps or hurts readability.
Press Check my work.

checks.label: Item 1 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Headings let people and screen readers jump to a section.

checks.label: Item 2 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Low contrast is hard to read, especially for low vision.

checks.label: Item 3 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Alternative text tells people who cannot see the picture what it shows.

checks.label: Item 4 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Capitals are slower to read and sound shouty.

checks.label: Item 5 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Clear language is easier for every reader.

checks.label: Item 6 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Describe where a link goes instead, so it makes sense on its own.

checks.label: Item 7 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Text that is too small strains the eyes.

checks.label: Item 8 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Some people cannot tell the colours apart; add words or symbols too.

items.text: Clear headings in order
items.why: Headings let people and screen readers jump to a section.

items.text: Light grey text on a white background
items.why: Low contrast is hard to read, especially for low vision.

items.text: A short description of each picture
items.why: Alternative text tells people who cannot see the picture what it shows.

items.text: All text in capitals
items.why: Capitals are slower to read and sound shouty.

items.text: Plain language and short sentences
items.why: Clear language is easier for every reader.

items.text: Links that say click here
items.why: Describe where a link goes instead, so it makes sense on its own.

items.text: A readable font size, such as 11 or 12 points
items.why: Text that is too small strains the eyes.

items.text: Information shown only by colour
items.why: Some people cannot tell the colours apart; add words or symbols too.

activities.title: Final project: a short report
activities.objective: Bring headings, lists, a table and good writing together in one professional document.
activities.scenario: Your school wants a one-page report on how students travel to school, to help plan a bicycle shed. Write the report.
steps: Write a title as Heading 1.
Add sections: Summary, Findings, Recommendation (Heading 2).
Under Findings add a table with at least 4 rows and 2 columns showing how many students use each travel method.
Add a bulleted list of at least three reasons students gave.
End with a short, clear recommendation.
Keep the whole report between 120 and 350 words.

checks.label: A title (Heading 1)
checks.hint: Use Heading 1 for the title.
checks.explain: One clear title tells the reader what the report is.

checks.label: Three sections (Heading 2)
checks.hint: Summary, Findings and Recommendation each get a Heading 2.
checks.explain: Sections make a report easy to navigate.

checks.label: Sections in order
checks.hint: Summary, then Findings, then Recommendation.
checks.explain: A report moves from overview to evidence to advice.

checks.label: A table with 4 rows and 2 columns
checks.hint: Insert a table with Travel method and Students columns.
checks.explain: A table presents counts clearly.

checks.label: A bulleted list of three reasons
checks.hint: Use the bullet button.
checks.explain: A list gives the reasons at a glance.

checks.label: Between 120 and 350 words
checks.hint: Add detail or trim until the length fits.
checks.explain: A short report is more likely to be read.

checks.label: Key words in bold
checks.hint: Make the most important numbers or words bold.
checks.explain: Bold helps skimming readers find the key points.
